approachQuestion.prompt:
Find the first unshared badge

Input: an array badges in arrival order. Return the index of the first entry whose value occurs exactly once in the entire array, or −1 if no such entry exists.

Example 1: badges = [6,2,6,9,2,4]. Output: 3. Example 2: badges = [5,5]. Output: −1. Example 3: badges = []. Output: −1. 0 ≤ n ≤ 200,000.

Constraints: input is immutable; all identifiers and numeric entries are signed 32-bit integers unless specified. Arithmetic uses signed 64-bit integers. Prefer the least expected running-time growth, then avoid unnecessary asymptotic auxiliary storage. Non-adversarial hashing of fixed-size integer keys/tuples has expected amortized constant cost.

options.text: Count every badge with a map, then scan the original array from left to right and return the first index whose final count is one.
options.feedback: Only completed counts establish global uniqueness; the second scan applies the required arrival-order tie-break.

options.text: Comparison-sort copied (value,index) records, find singleton-value runs, and return the smallest original index among them.
options.feedback: Singleton runs and original indices make this correct, but ordering records is removable with direct frequency lookup.

options.text: Scan left to right and return the first value not already seen.
options.feedback: For [6,2,6], index 0 is unseen when read but later repeats; the correct index is 1.

options.text: Count all values, then return the index of any map entry with count one.
options.feedback: Map iteration does not enforce arrival order. For [9,2], returning index 1 is invalid even though both labels are unique.

feedback.reason: Separate a global frequency condition from the source-order rule used to select the answer.
details: Build a complete value-frequency map. Scan the immutable input from the beginning, returning the first index with count one, or −1 after the scan.
An early singleton candidate can repeat later. Build complete frequencies first, then scan original order to find the earliest index whose final count is one.

“Count every badge with a map, then scan the original array from left to right and return the first index whose final count is one.”: Only completed counts establish global uniqueness; the second scan applies the required arrival-order tie-break.

“Comparison-sort copied (value,index) records, find singleton-value runs, and return the smallest original index among them.”: Singleton runs and original indices make this correct, but ordering records is removable with direct frequency lookup.
“Scan left to right and return the first value not already seen.”: For [6,2,6], index 0 is unseen when read but later repeats; the correct index is 1.
“Count all values, then return the index of any map entry with count one.”: Map iteration does not enforce arrival order. For [9,2], returning index 1 is invalid even though both labels are unique.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Find the first unshared badge — analyzed method”, n is input length and u is its number of distinct badges. Choose its time and auxiliary-space pair. Use the tightest standard bound for the worst legal input of size n, with expected time over non-adversarial hashing. Fixed-width integer and fixed-size tuple hash operations take expected amortized O(1); arithmetic, comparison and copying one integer take O(1). Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input and returned result, includes all maps, sets, temporary copies and call stacks. The method is iterative, with constant call-stack space.
constraints: Use the tightest standard bound for the worst legal input of size n, with expected time over non-adversarial hashing. Fixed-width integer and fixed-size tuple hash operations take expected amortized O(1); arithmetic, comparison and copying one integer take O(1). Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input and returned result, includes all maps, sets, temporary copies and call stacks. The method is iterative, with constant call-stack space.

options.text: Expected O(n + 1) time; O(u + 1) auxiliary space.
O(n log n + 1) time; O(n + 1) space.

feedback.reason: A frequency pass and ordered selection pass are both linear in input length.
details: Separate a global frequency condition from the source-order rule used to select the answer.
Two scans of at most n entries use expected constant-cost hash operations, so expected O(n+1).
O(u+1) for final counts and scalar state. No input copy or recursion is used.
“Expected O(n + 1) time; O(u + 1) auxiliary space.”: Correct under the stated expected/amortized hashing model.
“Expected O(n + 1) time; O(1) space.”: Complete frequencies require up to u map entries.
“O(n log n + 1) time; O(n + 1) space.”: The fixed method counts and rescans; it never sorts copied records.
“Expected O(n² + 1) time; O(u + 1) space.”: The second scan performs direct lookups, not nested full-input counts.
